subject: India State of Forest Report 2023 — the figures this site quotes
transcription: Read off the source PDF page by page, once, and COMMITTED. Every number below was located in the document and is quoted with its table number, so any claim on the site can be checked against the original in one step. scripts/fetch-forest-loss.mjs re-downloads the PDF and checks its SHA-256 against the value recorded here; it never rewrites these numbers. ISFR is biennial, so a change to the document is a human event.

source.name: Forest Survey of India, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
source.publication: India State of Forest Report 2023, Volume 1
source.authority: This is India's own official forest assessment. It is the number the Government of India reports to FAO, and therefore the number behind the international series as well.

cover.table: Table 2.3 — Forest and Tree Cover of India

definitions.forest_cover: All land more than one hectare with tree canopy density above 10 per cent, irrespective of ownership, legal status or species. A plantation counts. An orchard can count. This is why 'forest cover' and 'forest' are not the same word.
definitions.tree_cover: Patches of trees outside the recorded forest area smaller than one hectare, including scattered trees in rural and urban settings.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition is the reason two honest sources disagree about whether India is gaining or losing forest. It measures canopy, not ecosystem.

change_2021_to_2023.table: Table 2.2 and the paragraph following it
change_2021_to_2023.quote: There has been a net increase of 156.41 km2 in the Forest Cover at national level.
change_2021_to_2023.the_arithmetic: A net figure hides its own components. The national net gain is 156.41 km2. Madhya Pradesh alone lost 371.54 km2 — more than twice the entire national net gain — and Mizoram alone gained 241.73 km2, more than the whole national net. Both statements are arithmetic on the report's own published numbers and neither is an interpretation.
change_2021_to_2023.the_scale: 156.41 km2 on a base of 715,342.61 km2 is a change of about two hundredths of one per cent. It is well inside what a mapping method can produce by changing nothing on the ground.

prone_classes.table: Table 4.14 — Forest Cover and Scrub in Different Fire Prone Classes
prone_classes.top_three_note: 1.45 + 9.89 + 16.63. Computed from the report's own column, not quoted from it.

burnt_area.the_comparison: 34,562.33 km2 burnt in one season against a total forest cover and scrub of 758,965.25 km2 is 4.55 per cent. This is a burnt AREA — a measured extent — and it is a different and larger kind of statement than a count of satellite detections.
burnt_area.why_it_outranks_a_detection_count: A detection is an event in a pixel. A burnt area is an extent, mapped afterwards from Landsat using differenced burn ratios. This is the forest-specific measurement that a FIRMS detection count is not, and it is made by the agency with the legal mandate.

alerts.note: FSI runs India's own forest fire alert system. It has no public API, so this site links it and never scrapes it.

holes: ISFR is biennial, so the newest official figure can be up to two years old. There is no monthly or annual official series.
The report gives no gross loss and no gross gain at national level — only a net, plus per-state changes. So national gross deforestation cannot be computed from it.

'Forest cover' includes plantations and orchards. The report does not publish a natural-forest-only series, so the question most readers are actually asking cannot be answered from this document alone.
The Forest (Conservation) Act diversion figures — how much forest land was legally cleared, with central approval — are published by the Ministry, not by FSI, and are not in this report.
